CHAPTER 13 - NUTRITION AND DIGESTION

Introduction

All living organisms need a continuous supply of energy and raw materials to grow, repair worn-out parts, carry out life processes and reproduce. This energy and these materials come from FOOD. NUTRITION is the sum of all the processes by which an organism takes in food, breaks it down, absorbs the useful products and uses them, while getting rid of the undigested waste. The substances in food that the body needs are called NUTRIENTS. This chapter looks at the different modes of nutrition, the components of a balanced diet, the structure of the human digestive system, how carbohydrates, proteins and fats are digested step by step by enzymes, how the products are absorbed and assimilated, and the disorders that arise when nutrition goes wrong.

13.1 TYPES OF NUTRITION

Living organisms obtain food in two broad ways.

AUTOTROPHIC NUTRITION ("self-feeding"): Green plants, algae and some bacteria make their own organic food from simple inorganic raw materials. In PHOTOSYNTHESIS, green plants use carbon dioxide and water in the presence of sunlight and the green pigment chlorophyll to build glucose, releasing oxygen. Autotrophs are the PRODUCERS of the living world - the ultimate source of food for all other organisms.

HETEROTROPHIC NUTRITION ("other-feeding"): Animals, fungi and most bacteria cannot make their own food; they depend, directly or indirectly, on autotrophs. There are three main types of heterotrophic nutrition:
 - HOLOZOIC nutrition: the organism takes in solid or liquid food, digests it inside the body, absorbs the products and egests the waste. Most animals, including humans, Amoeba and Hydra, are holozoic. It involves ingestion, digestion, absorption, assimilation and egestion.
 - SAPROPHYTIC (saprotrophic) nutrition: the organism feeds on dead and decaying organic matter. It secretes digestive enzymes onto the food OUTSIDE the body (extracellular digestion) and then absorbs the dissolved products. Fungi such as Rhizopus (bread mould), mushrooms and many bacteria are saprophytes; they are important DECOMPOSERS that recycle nutrients.
 - PARASITIC nutrition: the organism (the parasite) lives on or inside another living organism (the host) and obtains food from it, usually harming the host. Examples are the roundworm Ascaris, tapeworm and the malarial parasite Plasmodium in animals, and Cuscuta (dodder) among plants.

13.2 COMPONENTS OF FOOD AND A BALANCED DIET

Food is made of several classes of nutrients, each with a special role.

CARBOHYDRATES are the body's main and cheapest source of ENERGY. They include sugars (glucose, sucrose, lactose) and complex carbohydrates such as starch (in rice, wheat, potatoes) and cellulose (dietary fibre). One gram of carbohydrate releases about 4 kilocalories of energy.

PROTEINS are the BODY-BUILDING nutrients. Made of amino acids, they are needed for growth, repair of tissues and the making of enzymes, hormones and antibodies. Rich sources are pulses, beans, milk, eggs, fish and meat. One gram of protein gives about 4 kilocalories.

FATS (lipids) are a CONCENTRATED source of energy, giving about 9 kilocalories per gram - more than twice that of carbohydrates. They also form a store of energy under the skin, insulate the body against cold and cushion internal organs. Sources include ghee, butter, oils, nuts and oily fish.

VITAMINS are needed only in tiny amounts but are essential to keep the body healthy and to regulate its processes. They are of two kinds: FAT-SOLUBLE vitamins (A, D, E, K) and WATER-SOLUBLE vitamins (the B-complex group and vitamin C). Each vitamin has a specific function, and its lack causes a particular deficiency disease.

MINERALS such as calcium, phosphorus, iron, iodine and sodium are inorganic nutrients needed for building bones and teeth (calcium, phosphorus), forming haemoglobin (iron), making the thyroid hormone (iodine) and maintaining the balance of body fluids.

WATER makes up about two-thirds of the body. It is the medium in which all reactions occur, it transports substances in blood, helps in digestion and absorption, and regulates body temperature. ROUGHAGE or dietary FIBRE (mainly cellulose) is not digested but adds bulk to the food, helps the movement of material through the gut and prevents constipation.

A BALANCED DIET is one that contains all the nutrients - carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals, water and roughage - in the RIGHT PROPORTIONS to meet the body's needs for energy, growth and health. The exact amounts depend on age, sex, activity and health. A diet lacking one or more nutrients, or containing them in wrong proportions, leads to MALNUTRITION.

13.3 MODES OF FEEDING IN ANIMALS

Animals feed in a variety of ways depending on their food. FILTER (or suspension) FEEDERS such as many aquatic animals sieve tiny food particles from water. FLUID FEEDERS such as mosquitoes, leeches and aphids suck fluids like blood or plant sap. SUBSTRATE FEEDERS like earthworms live in their food and eat their way through it. BULK FEEDERS, including most animals and humans, take in large pieces of food. On the basis of the food they eat, animals are HERBIVORES (plant eaters, e.g. cow, deer), CARNIVORES (flesh eaters, e.g. lion, tiger) or OMNIVORES (which eat both plants and animals, e.g. humans, crow).

13.4 THE HUMAN DIGESTIVE SYSTEM

The human digestive system has two parts: the ALIMENTARY CANAL - a long muscular tube running from the mouth to the anus - and the associated DIGESTIVE GLANDS that pour their secretions into it.

THE ALIMENTARY CANAL

MOUTH AND BUCCAL CAVITY: Food enters through the mouth into the buccal (oral) cavity. Here it is chewed by the TEETH and mixed with saliva. Humans have four kinds of teeth - incisors (for cutting), canines (for tearing), premolars and molars (for grinding) - an arrangement called HETERODONT dentition. Human beings form two sets of teeth in a lifetime (DIPHYODONT): milk teeth and permanent teeth. The muscular TONGUE mixes food with saliva, helps in swallowing and tasting, and rolls the food into a soft ball called a BOLUS. Three pairs of SALIVARY GLANDS pour saliva into the mouth.

PHARYNX AND OESOPHAGUS: The bolus is pushed into the PHARYNX and then into the OESOPHAGUS (food pipe), a muscular tube that carries food to the stomach by wave-like muscular contractions called PERISTALSIS. A flap called the EPIGLOTTIS closes the windpipe during swallowing so that food does not enter the respiratory passage.

STOMACH: The stomach is a wide, muscular, J-shaped bag. Its wall secretes GASTRIC JUICE and churns the food, mixing it thoroughly to form a semi-liquid paste called CHYME. Food usually stays in the stomach for a few hours. Rings of muscle called SPHINCTERS guard the openings at the top and bottom of the stomach.

SMALL INTESTINE: This is the longest part of the alimentary canal (about 6-7 metres, highly coiled) and the main site of digestion and absorption. It has three regions: the DUODENUM (the first C-shaped part, which receives bile from the liver and pancreatic juice from the pancreas), the JEJUNUM (the middle part) and the ILEUM (the last and longest part, where most absorption occurs). The inner lining is folded and covered with millions of tiny finger-like projections called VILLI.

LARGE INTESTINE: Undigested food passes into the large intestine, which is shorter but wider. It has the CAECUM (with the finger-like APPENDIX), the COLON and the RECTUM. The large intestine ABSORBS most of the remaining WATER and some salts from the undigested material, turning it into semi-solid faeces.

RECTUM AND ANUS: The faeces are stored temporarily in the RECTUM and finally passed out (egested) through the ANUS. This removal of undigested waste is called EGESTION or defecation.

13.5 DIGESTIVE GLANDS AND THEIR SECRETIONS

SALIVARY GLANDS: Three pairs (parotid, submandibular and sublingual) pour SALIVA into the mouth. Saliva moistens the food and contains the enzyme SALIVARY AMYLASE (ptyalin), which begins the digestion of starch. It also contains mucus and the germ-killing substance lysozyme.

GASTRIC GLANDS: Tiny glands in the wall of the stomach secrete GASTRIC JUICE, which contains HYDROCHLORIC ACID (HCl), the enzyme PEPSIN (secreted as inactive pepsinogen), and MUCUS. The HCl makes the stomach contents acidic, kills germs, and activates pepsinogen into pepsin. Mucus protects the stomach lining from being digested by its own acid and enzyme.

LIVER AND BILE: The LIVER is the largest gland in the body. It secretes a greenish-yellow fluid called BILE, which is stored in the GALL BLADDER and released into the duodenum. Bile contains NO enzymes; its bile salts EMULSIFY fats - breaking large fat droplets into tiny ones - so that fat-digesting enzymes can act on them more easily. Bile is alkaline and neutralises the acidic chyme coming from the stomach.

PANCREAS: The PANCREAS is a gland lying below the stomach. It secretes PANCREATIC JUICE into the duodenum. Pancreatic juice contains several enzymes: pancreatic AMYLASE (digests starch), TRYPSIN (digests proteins) and LIPASE (digests fats). It is alkaline because it contains sodium bicarbonate. The pancreas is a DUAL gland - it also makes the hormones insulin and glucagon that control blood sugar.

INTESTINAL GLANDS: Glands in the wall of the small intestine secrete INTESTINAL JUICE (succus entericus), which contains a mixture of enzymes such as maltase, sucrase, lactase, peptidases (erepsin) and intestinal lipase that complete the digestion of carbohydrates, proteins and fats.

13.6 DIGESTION OF FOOD

DIGESTION is the process by which large, insoluble food molecules are broken down, with the help of enzymes, into small, soluble molecules that the body can absorb. It begins in the mouth and is completed in the small intestine.

DIGESTION OF CARBOHYDRATES:
 - In the MOUTH, salivary amylase (ptyalin) begins breaking STARCH into the sugar MALTOSE.
 - In the STOMACH, this action stops because the acidic medium inactivates amylase.
 - In the SMALL INTESTINE, pancreatic amylase converts the remaining starch into maltose. Intestinal enzymes then finish the job: MALTASE splits maltose into glucose, SUCRASE splits sucrose into glucose and fructose, and LACTASE splits lactose into glucose and galactose. The end products are simple sugars (mainly GLUCOSE).

DIGESTION OF PROTEINS:
 - In the STOMACH, the enzyme PEPSIN (active in acidic conditions) breaks proteins into smaller fragments called PEPTONES and proteoses.
 - In the SMALL INTESTINE, pancreatic TRYPSIN continues breaking proteins and peptones into still smaller peptides. Intestinal PEPTIDASES (erepsin) finally split these peptides into AMINO ACIDS, the end products of protein digestion.

DIGESTION OF FATS:
 - Very little fat digestion occurs before the small intestine.
 - In the SMALL INTESTINE, BILE from the liver first EMULSIFIES the fat into tiny droplets. Then pancreatic and intestinal LIPASE break the emulsified fats into FATTY ACIDS and GLYCEROL, the end products of fat digestion.

Thus, by the time food reaches the end of the small intestine, carbohydrates have become simple sugars, proteins have become amino acids, and fats have become fatty acids and glycerol - all small, soluble and ready to be absorbed.

13.7 ABSORPTION AND ASSIMILATION

ABSORPTION is the passage of the digested food from the alimentary canal into the blood and lymph. It takes place mainly in the SMALL INTESTINE, which is beautifully adapted for it. Its inner surface bears millions of finger-like VILLI (singular villus). Each villus is thin-walled, richly supplied with blood capillaries and contains a small lymph vessel called a LACTEAL. The villi enormously INCREASE the surface area for absorption, and their thin walls and rich blood supply make absorption fast and efficient. Glucose, amino acids, minerals and water-soluble vitamins pass into the BLOOD capillaries of the villi, while fatty acids and glycerol enter the LACTEALS as tiny fat droplets and reach the blood through the lymph.

ASSIMILATION is the process by which the absorbed food is used by the body cells - to release energy (mainly from glucose), to build and repair tissues (from amino acids) and to store surplus food (as glycogen in the liver and muscles, or as fat under the skin). The absorbed nutrients are first carried to the LIVER.

ROLE OF THE LIVER: The liver is a remarkable chemical factory. It regulates the level of glucose in the blood by storing excess glucose as GLYCOGEN and releasing it when needed; it stores certain vitamins and iron; it converts excess amino acids into urea (deamination); it makes bile; and it detoxifies harmful substances such as alcohol and drugs.

EGESTION: The undigested and unabsorbed material passes into the large intestine, where most of the water is absorbed, and the remaining semi-solid faeces are stored in the rectum and finally removed through the anus. This removal of undigested waste is called EGESTION.

13.8 NUTRITIONAL DISORDERS

When the diet is unbalanced - too little, too much or lacking particular nutrients - MALNUTRITION results.

PROTEIN-ENERGY MALNUTRITION (PEM) occurs when the diet lacks enough proteins and/or total energy, and is common in children. It has two forms:
 - MARASMUS, caused by a severe deficiency of BOTH proteins and calories (total food). The child becomes extremely thin and weak, with wasted muscles, a shrunken "old-man" face and stunted growth.
 - KWASHIORKOR, caused by a deficiency of PROTEIN when calorie intake may be adequate. The child shows swelling (oedema) of the body, especially a swollen belly and legs, a puffy face, thin discoloured hair and poor growth.

OBESITY is the opposite problem - eating far more energy (especially fats and sugars) than the body uses, so the excess is stored as fat. It increases the risk of heart disease, high blood pressure and diabetes.

VITAMIN-DEFICIENCY DISEASES arise when particular vitamins are missing:
 - Vitamin A deficiency causes NIGHT BLINDNESS and dry eyes.
 - Vitamin D deficiency causes RICKETS in children (soft, bent bones) and osteomalacia in adults.
 - Vitamin B1 (thiamine) deficiency causes BERI-BERI.
 - Vitamin C deficiency causes SCURVY (bleeding, spongy gums).
 - Vitamin K deficiency leads to poor blood clotting.
MINERAL-DEFICIENCY conditions include ANAEMIA (iron deficiency, too little haemoglobin) and GOITRE (iodine deficiency, swelling of the thyroid gland). A balanced diet, rich in fresh fruits, vegetables, pulses and adequate proteins, prevents these disorders.

SUMMARY

- Nutrition is the intake and use of food; it is AUTOTROPHIC (self-made, as in green plants by photosynthesis) or HETEROTROPHIC (holozoic, saprophytic or parasitic).
- Food supplies carbohydrates (energy, 4 kcal/g), proteins (body-building, amino acids), fats (concentrated energy, 9 kcal/g), vitamins, minerals, water and roughage. A balanced diet has all of these in the right proportions.
- The human digestive system is the alimentary canal (mouth and buccal cavity with teeth and tongue, pharynx, oesophagus, stomach, small intestine - duodenum, jejunum, ileum -, large intestine, rectum, anus) plus digestive glands.
- Digestive glands: salivary glands (salivary amylase), gastric glands (HCl, pepsin, mucus), liver (bile - emulsifies fats), pancreas (amylase, trypsin, lipase) and intestinal glands (maltase, sucrase, lactase, peptidases, lipase).
- Digestion: starch -> maltose -> glucose (amylase, maltase); proteins -> peptones -> amino acids (pepsin, trypsin, peptidases); fats -> emulsified by bile -> fatty acids and glycerol (lipase). Most digestion is completed in the small intestine.
- Absorption occurs mainly in the small intestine through the villi, which increase surface area; glucose and amino acids enter the blood, fatty acids and glycerol enter the lacteals.
- Assimilation is the use of absorbed food for energy, growth and storage; the liver stores glucose as glycogen, forms urea and detoxifies. Undigested waste is egested through the anus.
- Nutritional disorders: PEM (marasmus - lack of protein and calories; kwashiorkor - lack of protein), obesity, and vitamin/mineral deficiency diseases (night blindness, rickets, beri-beri, scurvy, anaemia, goitre).

worksheet.title: Worksheet - Nutrition and Digestion (NIOS Senior Secondary Biology)
worksheet.instructions: Attempt all questions. Answer short-answer questions in 2-3 sentences and long-answer questions in detail. Draw labelled diagrams where helpful.

questions.question: Define nutrition and distinguish between autotrophic and heterotrophic nutrition with one example of each.
questions.answer:
Nutrition is the sum of all processes by which an organism takes in food, breaks it down, absorbs the useful products and uses them for energy, growth and repair.

Autotrophic nutrition: the organism makes its own organic food from simple inorganic substances. Example: green plants, which build glucose from carbon dioxide and water using sunlight and chlorophyll (photosynthesis).

Heterotrophic nutrition: the organism cannot make its own food and depends on ready-made organic food. Example: animals such as human beings (and also fungi and most bacteria).
questions.explanation: Definition + autotrophic (plants) vs heterotrophic (animals).

questions.question: Name the six main components of food and give one function of each.
questions.answer:
Carbohydrates - the main source of energy (4 kcal/g).
Proteins - body building, growth and repair of tissues (made of amino acids).
Fats - a concentrated store of energy (9 kcal/g) and insulation.
Vitamins - regulate body processes and prevent deficiency diseases.
Minerals - build bones and teeth, form haemoglobin and hormones.
Water - the medium for reactions, transport and temperature control (roughage/fibre adds bulk and prevents constipation).
questions.explanation: Six nutrients with one function each.

questions.question: Trace the path of food through the human alimentary canal, naming the parts in order.
questions.answer: Food passes in this order: mouth (buccal cavity, with teeth and tongue) -> pharynx -> oesophagus (food pipe) -> stomach -> small intestine (duodenum -> jejunum -> ileum) -> large intestine (caecum, colon) -> rectum -> anus. Food is moved along the canal by wave-like muscular contractions called peristalsis. Most digestion and absorption occur in the small intestine, while the large intestine absorbs water, and undigested waste is egested through the anus.
questions.explanation: Ordered path mouth to anus with peristalsis.

questions.question: Name the digestive glands in humans and state the main secretion of each.
questions.answer:
Salivary glands - secrete saliva (containing salivary amylase) into the mouth.
Gastric glands - secrete gastric juice (HCl, pepsin, mucus) in the stomach.
Liver - secretes bile (stored in the gall bladder), which emulsifies fats.
Pancreas - secretes pancreatic juice (amylase, trypsin, lipase) into the duodenum.
Intestinal glands - secrete intestinal juice with enzymes (maltase, sucrase, lactase, peptidases, lipase) that complete digestion.
questions.explanation: Five glands and their secretions.

questions.question: Describe the step-by-step digestion of carbohydrates in the human body, naming the enzymes, their sites of action and the end products.
questions.answer:
Carbohydrate digestion mainly means the digestion of starch.

1. Mouth: saliva contains salivary amylase (ptyalin), which begins breaking starch into the sugar maltose while food is chewed.

2. Stomach: the acidic gastric juice inactivates salivary amylase, so carbohydrate digestion largely stops here.

3. Small intestine (duodenum): pancreatic juice contains pancreatic amylase, which converts the remaining starch into maltose.

4. Small intestine (final step): intestinal juice supplies enzymes that finish digestion - maltase splits maltose into glucose, sucrase splits sucrose into glucose and fructose, and lactase splits lactose into glucose and galactose.

End products: simple sugars, mainly glucose, which are then absorbed through the villi into the blood. Thus carbohydrate digestion begins in the mouth and is completed in the small intestine.
questions.explanation: Starch -> maltose (amylase) -> glucose (maltase etc.); completed in small intestine.

questions.question: What is the role of hydrochloric acid and bile in digestion?
questions.answer:
Hydrochloric acid (HCl) in the gastric juice makes the stomach contents acidic, kills germs taken in with food, and activates the inactive pepsinogen into the active enzyme pepsin so that protein digestion can begin.

Bile, secreted by the liver, contains no enzymes. It is alkaline, so it neutralises the acidic chyme entering the duodenum, and its bile salts emulsify fats - breaking large fat droplets into tiny ones - which greatly increases the surface area on which lipase can act, making fat digestion faster.
questions.explanation: HCl: acid medium, kills germs, activates pepsin; bile: neutralises and emulsifies fat.

questions.question: Describe the structure of a villus and explain how the small intestine is adapted for absorption.
questions.answer:
Absorption is the passage of digested food from the alimentary canal into the blood and lymph, and it occurs mainly in the small intestine.

Structure of a villus: the inner lining of the small intestine is folded and bears millions of tiny finger-like projections called villi. Each villus is thin-walled (one cell thick), richly supplied with blood capillaries, and contains a small lymph vessel called a lacteal.

Adaptations for absorption:
1. The great number of villi (and micro-folds) enormously increases the surface area for absorption.
2. The very thin walls allow digested food to pass through quickly.
3. The rich network of blood capillaries carries absorbed glucose, amino acids, minerals and water-soluble vitamins away rapidly into the blood.
4. The lacteals absorb fatty acids and glycerol as tiny fat droplets and pass them into the lymph.
5. The small intestine is very long and highly coiled, giving more time and area for absorption.

Together these features make absorption fast and efficient.
questions.explanation: Villus = thin wall, capillaries, lacteal; large surface area, long coiled intestine.

questions.question: Distinguish between marasmus and kwashiorkor.
questions.answer:
Both are forms of protein-energy malnutrition (PEM) seen in children.

Marasmus is caused by a severe deficiency of BOTH proteins and calories (total food). The child becomes extremely thin and weak, with wasted muscles, a shrunken 'old-man' face and badly stunted growth.

Kwashiorkor is caused mainly by a deficiency of PROTEIN, even when the calorie intake may be adequate (a starchy diet). The child shows swelling (oedema) of the body - a swollen belly and legs, a puffy face - along with thin, discoloured hair and poor growth.
questions.explanation: Marasmus: protein + calorie lack, thin; kwashiorkor: protein lack, oedema.

questions.question: How is a saprophyte different from a parasite? Give one example of each.
questions.answer:
A saprophyte obtains food from dead and decaying organic matter, secreting digestive enzymes onto the food outside its body and then absorbing the dissolved products; it does not harm any living host. Example: the fungus Rhizopus (bread mould).

A parasite obtains food from a living organism (the host) on or inside which it lives, and usually harms the host. Example: the tapeworm (or Cuscuta among plants).
questions.explanation: Saprophyte - dead matter; parasite - living host.

questions.question: Explain the role of the liver in the body and describe assimilation of digested food.
questions.answer:
Assimilation is the process by which the absorbed food is used by the body cells - glucose is oxidised to release energy, amino acids are used to build and repair tissues and make enzymes and hormones, and surplus food is stored (as glycogen or as fat). The absorbed nutrients are first carried to the liver.

Role of the liver (the largest gland in the body):
1. It regulates blood glucose by storing excess glucose as glycogen and releasing it as glucose when the body needs energy.
2. It stores certain vitamins (such as A and D) and iron.
3. It converts excess amino acids into urea (deamination), which is then excreted.
4. It makes bile, which helps in the digestion of fats.
5. It detoxifies harmful substances such as alcohol and drugs.

Thus the liver is a central chemical factory that manages the absorbed nutrients and keeps the internal environment balanced, while assimilation puts those nutrients to work for energy, growth and storage.

questions.question: What is holozoic nutrition? Name the processes involved.
questions.answer: Holozoic nutrition is the mode of heterotrophic nutrition in which an organism takes in solid or liquid food, digests it inside its body, absorbs the useful products and egests the undigested waste. It involves five processes: ingestion (taking in food), digestion (breaking it down), absorption (taking up the products), assimilation (using them) and egestion (removing the waste). Most animals, including humans and Amoeba, are holozoic.
questions.explanation: Holozoic = ingest, digest, absorb, assimilate, egest.

questions.question: Compare saprophytic and parasitic nutrition with examples.
questions.answer:
Saprophytic nutrition: the organism feeds on dead and decaying organic matter. It secretes digestive enzymes onto the food outside its body (extracellular digestion) and absorbs the dissolved products. It harms no living host and acts as a decomposer. Example: the fungus Rhizopus and mushrooms.

Parasitic nutrition: the organism (parasite) lives on or inside a living organism (host) and takes food from it, usually harming the host. Example: the tapeworm and roundworm in animals, and Cuscuta among plants.

So saprophytes feed on dead matter while parasites feed on living hosts.
questions.explanation: Saprophyte - dead matter, decomposer; parasite - living host, harmful.

questions.question: Why do we need proteins in our diet? Name two sources.
questions.answer: Proteins are the body-building nutrients. They are needed for the growth of the body, the repair of worn-out tissues, and the making of enzymes, hormones and antibodies. They are built from amino acids. Two good sources are pulses (dals) and milk (also eggs, fish and meat).
questions.explanation: Proteins build/repair tissues; sources pulses, milk.

questions.question: What is a balanced diet? Why is it important?
questions.answer:
A balanced diet is one that contains all the nutrients - carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals, water and roughage - in the right proportions to meet the body's needs for energy, growth, repair and good health. The exact amounts depend on a person's age, sex, activity and health.

It is important because each nutrient has a special role: carbohydrates and fats give energy, proteins build the body, vitamins and minerals regulate processes and prevent deficiency diseases, water is the medium for all reactions, and roughage keeps the gut working. A diet lacking or unbalanced in these nutrients leads to malnutrition and disease.
questions.explanation: All nutrients in right proportion; prevents malnutrition.

questions.question: State two functions of water and one function of minerals in the body.
questions.answer: Functions of water: (1) it is the medium in which all the body's chemical reactions and digestion take place and it transports substances in the blood; (2) it helps to regulate body temperature (for example through sweating). Function of minerals: minerals such as calcium and phosphorus build strong bones and teeth (iron forms haemoglobin, iodine makes the thyroid hormone).
questions.explanation: Water: reaction medium/transport, temperature; minerals: bones/teeth etc.

questions.question: Name the different types of human teeth and their functions.
questions.answer: Humans have four kinds of teeth (heterodont dentition): incisors, at the front, for cutting and biting food; canines, for tearing and holding; premolars, for crushing; and molars, at the back, for grinding and chewing food. This variety lets us handle many kinds of food.
questions.explanation: Incisors cut, canines tear, premolars/molars grind.

questions.question: Describe the structure and function of the stomach.
questions.answer:
The stomach is a wide, muscular, J-shaped bag - the widest part of the alimentary canal. Its openings are guarded by rings of muscle called sphincters. The wall of the stomach has gastric glands that secrete gastric juice (hydrochloric acid, pepsin and mucus).

Functions: the muscular wall churns and mixes the food with gastric juice, turning it into a semi-liquid paste called chyme. The HCl kills germs and provides the acidic medium in which pepsin begins the digestion of proteins into peptones, while mucus protects the stomach lining from its own acid. Food is stored here for a few hours before passing on to the small intestine.
questions.explanation: J-shaped muscular bag; churns food, gastric juice, pepsin digests protein.

questions.question: What are the functions of the large intestine?
questions.answer: The large intestine is shorter but wider than the small intestine and has the caecum, colon and rectum. It does not take part in digestion. Its main function is to absorb most of the remaining water and some salts from the undigested food, turning it into semi-solid faeces. These faeces are stored temporarily in the rectum and finally egested through the anus.
questions.explanation: Absorbs water/salts; forms and stores faeces.

questions.question: Why is the small intestine considered the most important part of the digestive system?
questions.answer: The small intestine is the most important part because BOTH the completion of digestion and almost all absorption take place here. It receives bile from the liver and pancreatic juice from the pancreas in its first part, the duodenum, and its own intestinal juice supplies more enzymes. Together these complete the digestion of carbohydrates (to glucose), proteins (to amino acids) and fats (to fatty acids and glycerol). The small intestine is very long (about 6-7 m) and highly coiled, and its inner lining bears millions of villi that give a huge surface area for absorbing the digested food into the blood and lacteals. Because both digestion is finished and nutrients are taken up here, it is the key organ of the system.
questions.explanation: Digestion completed + absorption via villi occur here.

questions.question: What is bile? State its role in digestion.
questions.answer: Bile is a greenish-yellow alkaline fluid secreted by the liver and stored in the gall bladder, from where it is released into the duodenum. Bile contains no digestive enzymes. Its roles are: (1) its bile salts emulsify fats - breaking large fat droplets into tiny ones so that lipase can act on them easily; and (2) being alkaline, it neutralises the acidic chyme coming from the stomach, making the medium suitable for pancreatic and intestinal enzymes.
questions.explanation: Bile from liver; emulsifies fat, neutralises acid; no enzymes.

questions.question: Describe the composition and functions of gastric juice.
questions.answer:
Gastric juice is secreted by the gastric glands in the wall of the stomach. It contains three main components:
1. Hydrochloric acid (HCl) - makes the stomach contents acidic, kills germs taken in with food, and activates pepsinogen into the active enzyme pepsin.
2. Pepsin - an enzyme (secreted as inactive pepsinogen) that begins the digestion of proteins into peptones and proteoses in the acidic medium.
3. Mucus - protects the stomach lining from being digested by its own acid and enzyme.
Together these begin protein digestion and protect the stomach.
questions.explanation: HCl, pepsin, mucus and their roles.

questions.question: Why is the pancreas called a dual gland?
questions.answer: The pancreas is called a dual gland because it works both as an exocrine gland and as an endocrine gland. As an exocrine gland it secretes pancreatic juice (containing amylase, trypsin and lipase) through a duct into the duodenum to help digestion. As an endocrine gland it secretes the hormones insulin and glucagon directly into the blood to control the level of glucose in the body.
questions.explanation: Exocrine (digestive juice) + endocrine (insulin, glucagon).

questions.question: List the enzymes present in pancreatic juice and the food each acts on.
questions.answer: Pancreatic juice contains three main enzymes: pancreatic amylase, which digests starch (carbohydrate) into maltose; trypsin, which digests proteins and peptones into smaller peptides; and lipase, which digests emulsified fats into fatty acids and glycerol. The juice is alkaline (it contains sodium bicarbonate), which suits the action of these enzymes in the small intestine.
questions.explanation: Amylase-starch, trypsin-protein, lipase-fat.

questions.question: Explain the digestion of proteins step by step.
questions.answer:
Protein digestion happens in two main sites:
1. Stomach: the enzyme pepsin, active in the acidic medium created by HCl, breaks proteins into smaller fragments called peptones and proteoses.
2. Small intestine: pancreatic trypsin continues to break these proteins and peptones into still smaller peptides. Finally, intestinal peptidases (erepsin) split the peptides into amino acids.
The end product of protein digestion is amino acids, which are absorbed through the villi into the blood.
questions.explanation: Pepsin -> peptones; trypsin -> peptides; peptidases -> amino acids.

questions.question: Describe the digestion of fats in the human body.
questions.answer: Very little fat digestion occurs before the small intestine. In the small intestine, bile from the liver first emulsifies the fat - its bile salts break large fat droplets into many tiny droplets, greatly increasing the surface area. Then the enzyme lipase, from pancreatic juice and intestinal juice, breaks the emulsified fats into fatty acids and glycerol, which are the end products of fat digestion. These are absorbed into the lacteals of the villi.
questions.explanation: Bile emulsifies; lipase gives fatty acids + glycerol.

questions.question: Trace what happens to a piece of bread (rich in starch) as it passes through the alimentary canal.
questions.answer: In the mouth, the bread is chewed by the teeth and mixed with saliva; salivary amylase begins converting its starch into maltose, and the tongue rolls it into a bolus that is swallowed. In the oesophagus, peristalsis carries the bolus to the stomach, where the acidic gastric juice stops amylase action (bread has little protein or fat to digest here). In the small intestine, pancreatic amylase turns the remaining starch into maltose, and intestinal maltase splits maltose into glucose. The glucose is absorbed through the villi into the blood, carried to the liver and cells for energy, while any undigested residue (fibre) passes on to the large intestine and is finally egested.
questions.explanation: Mouth amylase -> stomach halts -> small intestine to glucose -> absorbed.

questions.question: Why does starch digestion stop in the stomach but restart in the small intestine?
questions.answer: In the mouth, salivary amylase begins digesting starch to maltose. When the food reaches the stomach, the hydrochloric acid makes the medium strongly acidic, which inactivates salivary amylase, so starch digestion stops there. In the small intestine, bile and the alkaline pancreatic juice neutralise the acid, and pancreatic amylase (which works in an alkaline medium) again acts on the starch, so digestion restarts and is completed by intestinal enzymes.
questions.explanation: Acid inactivates amylase; alkaline intestine lets amylase act again.

questions.question: An enzyme that works in the mouth becomes inactive in the stomach but a stomach enzyme works well there. Explain with reference to pH.
questions.answer: Enzymes work best at a particular pH (optimum pH). Salivary amylase, which acts in the mouth, works best in a neutral to slightly alkaline medium. The stomach is strongly acidic because of hydrochloric acid, so salivary amylase becomes inactive there. Pepsin, the stomach enzyme, has its optimum in an acidic medium, so the same acidic conditions that stop amylase actually suit pepsin, allowing it to digest proteins efficiently. This shows that each enzyme has its own suitable pH, and a medium that suits one may inactivate another.
questions.explanation: Amylase optimum neutral; pepsin optimum acidic; pH decides activity.

questions.question: What is the difference between absorption and assimilation?
questions.answer:
Absorption is the passage of the digested food (glucose, amino acids, fatty acids, glycerol, minerals, vitamins and water) from the alimentary canal, mainly the small intestine, into the blood and lymph through the villi.

Assimilation is the process that follows - the absorbed food is carried to the body cells and used there: glucose is oxidised to release energy, amino acids build and repair tissues, and surplus food is stored. So absorption is taking the food into the blood, while assimilation is using it in the cells.
questions.explanation: Absorption = into blood; assimilation = use by cells.

questions.question: Describe the role of the liver in the body.
questions.answer: The liver is the largest gland in the body and acts as a chemical factory. Its roles include: (1) regulating blood glucose by storing excess glucose as glycogen and releasing glucose when needed; (2) storing certain vitamins (such as A and D) and iron; (3) converting excess amino acids into urea (deamination) for excretion; (4) making bile, which helps digest fats; and (5) detoxifying harmful substances such as alcohol and drugs. In these ways the liver manages the absorbed nutrients and keeps the body's internal chemistry balanced.
questions.explanation: Glycogen store, urea, bile, detox, storage of vitamins/iron.

questions.question: Bile contains no enzyme, yet it is essential for fat digestion. Explain.
questions.answer: Bile contains no digestive enzyme, so it does not itself break down fat chemically. However, fats are insoluble in water and form large droplets on which the fat-digesting enzyme lipase can act only slowly. The bile salts in bile emulsify the fat - they break the large droplets into many tiny droplets, hugely increasing the total surface area exposed to lipase. As a result lipase can digest the fat much faster. So although bile is not an enzyme, it makes efficient fat digestion possible.
questions.explanation: Bile emulsifies fat, increasing surface area for lipase.

questions.question: Name any three vitamin deficiency diseases and the vitamin lacking in each.
questions.answer:
Three vitamin deficiency diseases are:
1. Night blindness - caused by the deficiency of vitamin A.
2. Rickets (soft, bent bones in children) - caused by the deficiency of vitamin D.
3. Scurvy (bleeding, spongy gums) - caused by the deficiency of vitamin C.
(Beri-beri, caused by lack of vitamin B1, is another example.) These can be prevented by a balanced diet rich in fresh fruits and vegetables.
questions.explanation: A - night blindness, D - rickets, C - scurvy.

questions.question: Explain the different types of nutrition found in living organisms with examples.
questions.answer:
Living organisms obtain food in two broad ways.

1. Autotrophic nutrition ('self-feeding'): the organism makes its own organic food from simple inorganic raw materials. Green plants, algae and some bacteria are autotrophs. In photosynthesis, green plants use carbon dioxide and water in the presence of sunlight and chlorophyll to build glucose and release oxygen. Autotrophs are the producers, the ultimate source of food for all others.

2. Heterotrophic nutrition ('other-feeding'): animals, fungi and most bacteria cannot make their own food and depend on autotrophs. It has three types:
(a) Holozoic - solid food is ingested, digested inside the body, absorbed and the waste egested (humans, Amoeba, Hydra).
(b) Saprophytic - the organism feeds on dead, decaying matter by external digestion and absorbs the products (fungi such as Rhizopus); these are decomposers.
(c) Parasitic - the organism lives on or in a living host and takes food from it, harming the host (tapeworm, Ascaris; Cuscuta among plants).

Thus nutrition ranges from self-made food in plants to holozoic, saprophytic and parasitic feeding in other organisms.
questions.explanation: Autotrophic (photosynthesis) vs heterotrophic (holozoic, saprophytic, parasitic).

questions.question: Describe the components of food, giving the function and one source of each.
questions.answer:
Food is made of several classes of nutrients:
1. Carbohydrates - the main and cheapest source of energy (about 4 kcal/g). Source: rice, wheat, potatoes.
2. Proteins - body-building nutrients for growth and repair and for making enzymes, hormones and antibodies; made of amino acids. Source: pulses, milk, eggs, fish, meat.
3. Fats - a concentrated store of energy (about 9 kcal/g), insulation and protection of organs. Source: ghee, butter, oils, nuts.
4. Vitamins - needed in tiny amounts to regulate body processes and prevent deficiency diseases; fat-soluble (A, D, E, K) and water-soluble (B-complex, C). Source: fruits and vegetables.
5. Minerals - inorganic nutrients such as calcium and phosphorus (bones and teeth), iron (haemoglobin) and iodine (thyroid hormone). Source: milk, green vegetables, salt.
6. Water - forms about two-thirds of the body, is the medium for reactions, transports substances and controls temperature. Source: drinking water, fruits.
Roughage (fibre), though not digested, adds bulk and prevents constipation. A balanced diet contains all of these in the right proportions.
questions.explanation: Six nutrients + roughage with functions and sources.

questions.question: Describe the human alimentary canal from mouth to anus, naming each part and its role.
questions.answer:
The alimentary canal is a long muscular tube running from the mouth to the anus.
1. Mouth and buccal cavity: food is chewed by the teeth (incisors, canines, premolars, molars) and mixed with saliva; the tongue mixes it and rolls it into a bolus; salivary amylase begins starch digestion.
2. Pharynx and oesophagus: the bolus is swallowed into the pharynx and pushed down the oesophagus to the stomach by peristalsis; the epiglottis closes the windpipe during swallowing.
3. Stomach: a J-shaped muscular bag that churns food and mixes it with gastric juice (HCl, pepsin, mucus) to form chyme; protein digestion begins here.
4. Small intestine (duodenum, jejunum, ileum): the longest part; receives bile and pancreatic juice in the duodenum; digestion is completed and most absorption occurs through the villi.
5. Large intestine (caecum, colon, rectum): absorbs most of the remaining water and salts, forming semi-solid faeces.
6. Rectum and anus: faeces are stored in the rectum and finally egested through the anus.
Food is moved along the whole canal by peristalsis.
questions.explanation: Ordered description of each part and its role.

questions.question: Describe the digestive glands of humans and the secretions and enzymes each produces.
questions.answer:
The digestive glands pour their secretions into the alimentary canal.
1. Salivary glands: three pairs pour saliva into the mouth. Saliva contains salivary amylase (ptyalin), which begins starch digestion, plus mucus and germ-killing lysozyme.
2. Gastric glands: in the stomach wall, they secrete gastric juice containing hydrochloric acid (acidic medium, kills germs, activates pepsin), pepsin (begins protein digestion) and mucus (protects the lining).
3. Liver: the largest gland; secretes bile (stored in the gall bladder). Bile has no enzymes but emulsifies fats and neutralises acidic chyme.
4. Pancreas: secretes pancreatic juice into the duodenum, containing amylase (starch), trypsin (protein) and lipase (fat); it is alkaline and is also a dual gland making insulin and glucagon.
5. Intestinal glands: in the small intestine wall, they secrete intestinal juice with enzymes such as maltase, sucrase, lactase, peptidases and lipase that complete digestion.
Together these glands supply the enzymes and conditions needed to digest all the food.
questions.explanation: Salivary, gastric, liver, pancreas, intestinal glands + secretions.

questions.question: Give a complete account of the digestion of carbohydrates, proteins and fats, stating the enzymes, sites and end products.
questions.answer:
Digestion breaks large insoluble food molecules into small soluble ones.

Carbohydrates: In the mouth, salivary amylase begins converting starch to maltose. In the stomach the acid inactivates amylase, so digestion pauses. In the small intestine, pancreatic amylase converts remaining starch to maltose, and intestinal enzymes finish the job - maltase (maltose to glucose), sucrase (sucrose to glucose and fructose) and lactase (lactose to glucose and galactose). End product: glucose (simple sugars).

Proteins: In the stomach, pepsin (in the acidic medium) breaks proteins into peptones. In the small intestine, pancreatic trypsin breaks these into peptides, and intestinal peptidases split peptides into amino acids. End product: amino acids.

Fats: Little digestion occurs before the small intestine. There, bile emulsifies fats into tiny droplets, and lipase (from pancreas and intestine) breaks the emulsified fats into fatty acids and glycerol. End product: fatty acids and glycerol.

Thus digestion begins in the mouth (carbohydrates) and stomach (proteins) but is completed for all three in the small intestine, giving glucose, amino acids, and fatty acids and glycerol.
questions.explanation: Full three-nutrient account: enzymes, sites, end products.

questions.question: Explain how enzymes, hydrochloric acid and bile work together to bring about digestion in the alimentary canal.
questions.answer:
Digestion depends on enzymes acting at the right site and pH, aided by HCl and bile.

Enzymes: each enzyme acts on one type of food. Amylase (in saliva and pancreatic juice) digests starch to sugars; pepsin and trypsin digest proteins to peptones, peptides and amino acids; lipase digests fats to fatty acids and glycerol. Enzymes act best at their own optimum pH.

Hydrochloric acid: secreted by the gastric glands, it makes the stomach acidic. This acid kills germs, activates inactive pepsinogen into active pepsin, and provides the acidic medium pepsin needs. However, the acid inactivates salivary amylase, pausing starch digestion in the stomach.

Bile: from the liver, bile has no enzymes but is alkaline, so it neutralises the acidic chyme entering the duodenum, creating the alkaline conditions that pancreatic and intestinal enzymes need. Its bile salts emulsify fats into tiny droplets, greatly increasing the surface on which lipase can act.

So HCl sets up acidic conditions for pepsin in the stomach, bile then makes the intestine alkaline and emulsifies fat, and the enzymes act at each site to break the food into absorbable products. They work as a coordinated team.
questions.explanation: Enzyme specificity + HCl (activate pepsin) + bile (neutralise, emulsify).

questions.question: Describe absorption, assimilation and egestion, explaining how the small intestine is adapted for absorption.
questions.answer:
After digestion, the food must be taken up and used.

Absorption is the passage of digested food from the alimentary canal into the blood and lymph, occurring mainly in the small intestine. Its inner lining bears millions of finger-like villi. Each villus is thin-walled, richly supplied with blood capillaries and contains a lacteal (lymph vessel). Adaptations: the many villi give a huge surface area; the thin walls allow quick passage; the rich blood supply carries glucose, amino acids, minerals and water-soluble vitamins rapidly into the blood, while fatty acids and glycerol enter the lacteals. The long, coiled intestine adds still more area and time.

Assimilation is the use of the absorbed food by body cells - glucose is oxidised for energy, amino acids build and repair tissues, and surplus food is stored (glycogen in the liver and muscles, fat under the skin). The liver plays a key part, storing glucose as glycogen and forming urea.

Egestion is the removal of the undigested, unabsorbed food. It passes into the large intestine, where water is absorbed; the semi-solid faeces are stored in the rectum and passed out through the anus.

Thus absorption takes food into the body, assimilation puts it to use, and egestion removes the waste.
questions.explanation: Absorption (villi), assimilation (use/store), egestion (waste out).

questions.question: Describe the main nutritional disorders, their causes, symptoms and prevention.
questions.answer:
Nutritional disorders arise when the diet is unbalanced.

1. Protein-energy malnutrition (PEM), common in children, has two forms:
(a) Marasmus - caused by severe deficiency of both proteins and calories; the child becomes extremely thin and weak, with wasted muscles, a shrunken 'old-man' face and stunted growth.
(b) Kwashiorkor - caused mainly by protein deficiency (calories may be adequate); the child shows swelling (oedema) of the belly and legs, a puffy face, thin discoloured hair and poor growth.

2. Obesity - caused by eating far more energy (fats and sugars) than the body uses, so the excess is stored as fat. It raises the risk of heart disease, high blood pressure and diabetes.

3. Vitamin and mineral deficiency diseases - vitamin A deficiency causes night blindness; vitamin D deficiency causes rickets; vitamin B1 deficiency causes beri-beri; vitamin C deficiency causes scurvy; iron deficiency causes anaemia; and iodine deficiency causes goitre.

Prevention: eating a balanced diet with adequate proteins, and rich in fresh fruits, vegetables and pulses, together with iodised salt, prevents these disorders.
questions.explanation: PEM (marasmus/kwashiorkor), obesity, deficiency diseases + prevention.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
Living organisms feed in different ways. Green plants make their own food using sunlight, while animals depend on ready-made food. Fungi grow on dead bread, and a tapeworm lives inside the human intestine taking food from it.
(a) What mode of nutrition do green plants show?
(b) Name the type of nutrition seen in fungi growing on dead bread.
(c) What type of nutrition does the tapeworm show, and what is the organism it lives in called?
(d) Why are green plants called producers?
questions.answer:
(a) Green plants show autotrophic nutrition - they make their own food by photosynthesis using carbon dioxide, water, sunlight and chlorophyll.
(b) Fungi growing on dead bread show saprophytic nutrition - they feed on dead, decaying matter by external digestion.
(c) The tapeworm shows parasitic nutrition; the organism it lives in and takes food from is called the host.
(d) Green plants are called producers because they produce organic food from simple inorganic substances, forming the ultimate source of food for all other organisms.
questions.explanation: Autotrophic; saprophytic; parasitic (host); producers.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
A nutritionist plans a school meal. Carbohydrates give about 4 kcal/g and fats about 9 kcal/g. She adds pulses and milk for growth, fruits and vegetables for regulation, and advises plenty of water and fibre.
(a) Which nutrient gives the most energy per gram?
(b) Why are pulses and milk added?
(c) What is the role of fruits and vegetables here?
(d) What is such a complete meal called?
questions.answer:
(a) Fat gives the most energy per gram - about 9 kcal/g, more than twice that of carbohydrate.
(b) Pulses and milk are protein-rich; they are added for the growth and repair of the body (body-building nutrients).
(c) Fruits and vegetables supply vitamins and minerals, which regulate body processes and prevent deficiency diseases; they also give roughage.
(d) A meal that contains all the nutrients in the right proportions is called a balanced diet.
questions.explanation: Fat 9 kcal; pulses/milk protein; fruits vitamins/minerals; balanced diet.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
When we eat a chapatti, it is chewed in the mouth and swallowed. It then travels down a muscular tube by wave-like contractions, is churned in a J-shaped bag, and moves into a long coiled tube where digestion is completed.
(a) Name the wave-like contractions that move food along.
(b) Name the J-shaped bag.
(c) Which long coiled tube completes digestion?
(d) Name the flap that stops food from entering the windpipe while swallowing.
questions.answer:
(a) The wave-like contractions are called peristalsis.
(b) The J-shaped bag is the stomach.
(c) Digestion is completed in the small intestine, a long coiled tube.
(d) The flap that stops food from entering the windpipe during swallowing is the epiglottis.
questions.explanation: Peristalsis; stomach; small intestine; epiglottis.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
Several glands help in digestion. One pours a juice with amylase into the mouth; another in the stomach wall secretes acid and pepsin; the largest gland makes a green fluid stored in a small sac; and a gland below the stomach pours a juice with three enzymes into the duodenum.
(a) Which gland pours amylase into the mouth?
(b) Name the acid secreted in the stomach.
(c) Which gland makes the green fluid, and where is it stored?
(d) Name the three enzymes of the gland below the stomach.
questions.answer:
(a) The salivary glands pour saliva (with salivary amylase) into the mouth.
(b) The acid secreted in the stomach is hydrochloric acid (HCl).
(c) The liver makes the green fluid (bile); it is stored in the gall bladder.
(d) The gland below the stomach is the pancreas; its three enzymes are amylase, trypsin and lipase.
questions.explanation: Salivary glands; HCl; liver/gall bladder; amylase, trypsin, lipase.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
During digestion, starch is first acted on in the mouth, protein digestion starts in the stomach, and fats are handled in the small intestine. Each food finally becomes a small, soluble molecule.
(a) Which enzyme starts starch digestion in the mouth?
(b) Name the enzyme that starts protein digestion and its site.
(c) What are the end products of fat digestion?
(d) Where is the digestion of all three completed?
questions.answer:
(a) Salivary amylase (ptyalin) starts starch digestion in the mouth.
(b) Pepsin starts protein digestion; its site is the stomach (in the acidic medium).
(c) The end products of fat digestion are fatty acids and glycerol.
(d) The digestion of all three foods is completed in the small intestine.
questions.explanation: Amylase; pepsin/stomach; fatty acids + glycerol; small intestine.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
A patient has his gall bladder removed and later complains of difficulty in digesting oily food. Bile normally has no enzymes but acts on fat, while lipase actually breaks fat down.
(a) What does bile do to fats?
(b) Why does removing bile storage affect fat digestion?
(c) Which enzyme actually digests fat, and from where does it come?
(d) In what medium (acidic or alkaline) does this enzyme work best?
questions.answer:
(a) Bile emulsifies fats - its bile salts break large fat droplets into many tiny droplets, increasing the surface area for enzyme action.
(b) Without stored bile released properly, fats are not emulsified well, so lipase cannot act efficiently and oily food is digested poorly.
(c) Lipase actually digests fat into fatty acids and glycerol; it comes from the pancreas (pancreatic juice) and the intestinal glands.
(d) Lipase works best in an alkaline medium, as found in the small intestine.
questions.explanation: Bile emulsifies; poor emulsification hinders lipase; lipase from pancreas; alkaline.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
The inner lining of the small intestine has millions of tiny finger-like projections. Each is thin-walled, has many blood capillaries and contains a lymph vessel. Digested food passes through these into the body and is then used by cells.
(a) Name these finger-like projections.
(b) Name the lymph vessel inside each.
(c) Which digested foods enter the blood, and which enter the lymph vessel?
(d) What name is given to the use of absorbed food by the cells?
questions.answer:
(a) The finger-like projections are called villi.
(b) The lymph vessel inside each villus is called the lacteal.
(c) Glucose, amino acids, minerals and water-soluble vitamins enter the blood capillaries; fatty acids and glycerol enter the lymph vessel (lacteal).
(d) The use of the absorbed food by the body cells is called assimilation.
questions.explanation: Villi; lacteal; glucose/amino acids to blood, fats to lacteal; assimilation.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
The liver is the largest gland in the body. It stores excess glucose, makes a fat-emulsifying fluid, converts excess amino acids into a nitrogen waste, and breaks down harmful substances.
(a) In what form does the liver store excess glucose?
(b) Name the fat-emulsifying fluid the liver makes.
(c) What nitrogen waste is formed from excess amino acids?
(d) State one more function of the liver.
questions.answer:
(a) The liver stores excess glucose in the form of glycogen.
(b) The fat-emulsifying fluid made by the liver is bile.
(c) Excess amino acids are converted into urea (by deamination).
(d) One more function: the liver detoxifies harmful substances such as alcohol and drugs (it also stores vitamins A and D and iron).
questions.explanation: Glycogen; bile; urea; detoxification/storage.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
In a village survey, one child is very thin with wasted muscles and an 'old-man' face; another has a swollen belly and puffy face; a third cannot see well in dim light; and a fourth has a swollen neck.
(a) Name the disorder in the very thin child.
(b) Name the disorder in the child with a swollen belly and puffy face, and the nutrient lacking.
(c) Which vitamin is deficient in the child who cannot see in dim light?
(d) What causes the swollen neck (goitre)?
questions.answer:
(a) The very thin child with wasted muscles and an 'old-man' face has marasmus (deficiency of both proteins and calories).
(b) The child with a swollen belly and puffy face has kwashiorkor; the nutrient lacking is protein.
(c) The child who cannot see in dim light (night blindness) is deficient in vitamin A.
(d) Goitre (swollen neck) is caused by the deficiency of iodine, which enlarges the thyroid gland.
questions.explanation: Marasmus; kwashiorkor (protein); vitamin A; iodine.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.
Two brothers eat very differently. One eats a lot of sweets, fried food and rich fats but avoids exercise; the other eats mostly polished rice with little else. Over time the first becomes very overweight, while the second becomes weak.
(a) What disorder is the first brother likely to develop, and why?
(b) Name two health risks linked with this disorder.
(c) Why might the second brother suffer from malnutrition?
(d) What single dietary change would most help both of them?
questions.answer:
(a) The first brother is likely to develop obesity, because he eats far more energy (fats and sugars) than his body uses, so the excess is stored as fat.
(b) Two health risks linked with obesity are heart disease and high blood pressure (diabetes is another).
(c) The second brother eats mainly polished rice (mostly carbohydrate) with little protein, vitamins or minerals, so his diet is unbalanced and he suffers from malnutrition.
(d) The single most helpful change is to eat a balanced diet - the first cutting down fats and sugars and exercising, the second adding proteins (pulses, milk), fruits and vegetables.
questions.explanation: Obesity from excess energy; heart disease/BP; unbalanced diet; balanced diet.
